Psalms 51.audience: The title links this psalm to David "when Nathan the prophet came unto him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba" (2 Samuel 12). It became one of the church's Penitential Psalms.

culture.title: Purge me with hyssop
culture.text: Hyssop, a small bushy plant, was used to sprinkle blood or water in cleansing rites for lepers and those defiled by a corpse (Leviticus 14:4–7; Numbers 19:18).

culture.title: Blotting out
culture.text: Ink on papyrus or leather could be washed or scraped off. "Blot out my transgressions" pictures a record erased.

Psalms 52.audience: The title links this psalm to the time "when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul" that David had visited the priests at Nob (1 Samuel 22:9–19).

culture.title: A sharp razor
culture.text: Doeg's tongue is "like a sharp razor, working deceitfully." Razors were used for shaving and also in vows and mourning rites.

culture.title: A green olive tree
culture.text: Olive trees can live for centuries and stay green year-round. Olive trees grew in temple courts and around houses.

Psalms 53.audience: Titled "upon Mahalath, Maschil, A Psalm of David." It is nearly identical to Psalm 14, but uses "God" (Elohim) instead of "the LORD," as most psalms in Book II do.

culture.title: Mahalath
culture.text: Mahalath is a musical term of uncertain meaning, perhaps a tune or a style of singing.

Psalms 54.audience: The title links this psalm to the Ziphims' report to Saul that David was hiding among them (1 Samuel 23:19).

culture.title: The wilderness of Ziph
culture.text: Ziph was a town in the hill country of Judah southeast of Hebron, near the rugged wilderness where David hid.

culture.title: A freewill offering
culture.text: A freewill offering was given voluntarily, not to fulfill a vow (Leviticus 7:16).

Psalms 55.audience: A psalm of David about betrayal by a close friend: "we took sweet counsel together, and walked unto the house of God in company" (Psalm 55:14).

culture.title: Wings of a dove
culture.text: Doves nest in the clefts of cliffs in the wilderness. The psalmist longs to fly away and be at rest.

culture.title: Prayer three times a day
culture.text: "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray." Daniel later prayed three times a day (Daniel 6:10).

Psalms 56.audience: The title links this psalm to the time "when the Philistines took him in Gath" (1 Samuel 21:10–15). It is titled Michtam and "upon Jonathelemrechokim," which the KJV margin renders ‘the dumb dove in far places,’ probably a tune.

culture.title: Tears in a bottle
culture.text: "Put thou my tears into thy bottle." Liquids were kept in skin bottles. The image is of God keeping a record of every tear.

Psalms 57.audience: The title links this psalm to David fleeing from Saul "in the cave" (1 Samuel 22:1; 24:3). Its title includes "Altaschith," ‘destroy not,’ also on Psalms 58, 59, and 75.

culture.title: Awaking the dawn
culture.text: "I myself will awake early"—in the Hebrew, ‘I will awaken the dawn,’ rising before sunrise to praise.

culture.title: Lions and fiery men
culture.text: Enemies with teeth like spears and arrows are pictured as lions—a common image for violent foes.

Psalms 58.audience: A Michtam of David addressed to unjust rulers or judges ("O congregation," Psalm 58:1).

culture.title: The deaf adder
culture.text: Snake charmers were known in the ancient Near East. The wicked are like an adder that refuses to listen to the charmer.

culture.title: A melting snail
culture.text: "As a snail which melteth"—snails leave a trail of slime and seem to dissolve in the heat.

Psalms 59.audience: The title links this psalm to the night "when Saul sent, and they watched the house to kill him" (1 Samuel 19:11).

culture.title: Dogs prowling the city
culture.text: Packs of half-wild dogs roamed city streets at night searching for scraps. David's enemies return each evening like them.

Psalms 60.audience: The title links this psalm to David's wars against Aram-naharaim and Aram-zobah, "when Joab returned, and smote of Edom in the valley of salt twelve thousand" (2 Samuel 8:13).

culture.title: Tribal names as God's possessions
culture.text: Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Judah are named as God's—Judah as his "lawgiver" (sceptre) and Ephraim as "the strength of mine head" (helmet).

culture.title: Casting a shoe
culture.text: "Over Edom will I cast out my shoe"—throwing a sandal over land may signify taking possession of it (compare Ruth 4:7).

culture.title: Moab my washpot
culture.text: A washpot was a basin for washing feet—a humble household use for a conquered enemy.

Psalms 61.audience: Titled "upon Neginah, A Psalm of David." The psalmist cries "from the end of the earth" and prays for the king's long life (Psalm 61:6).

culture.title: A rock higher than I
culture.text: High rocky outcrops gave safety from floods and enemies in Israel's hills.

culture.title: Daily vows
culture.text: Vows promised to God were paid with offerings and praise (Psalm 66:13).

Psalms 62.audience: Titled "to Jeduthun, A Psalm of David." It repeats "my soul waiteth upon God" and teaches trust in God rather than in wealth or power.

culture.title: A bowing wall
culture.text: Mud-brick and stone walls could lean and collapse after heavy rain. Enemies try to topple the psalmist like "a tottering fence."

culture.title: Weighed in the balance
culture.text: Goods were weighed on balance scales. Men of high and low degree together weigh "lighter than vanity."

Psalms 63.audience: Titled "A Psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Judah." The wilderness between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea is dry and barren.

culture.title: A dry and thirsty land
culture.text: The Judean wilderness receives very little rain. The psalmist's thirst for God is pictured as thirst in that land.

culture.title: Watches of the night
culture.text: The night was divided into watches. The psalmist meditates on God through them.

Psalms 64.audience: A psalm of David asking protection from the secret plots of enemies.

culture.title: Sharpened tongues
culture.text: Enemies "whet their tongue like a sword, and bend their bows to shoot their arrows, even bitter words."

Psalms 65.audience: A psalm and song of David praising God for a good harvest. It may have been sung at one of Israel's harvest festivals.

culture.title: The river of God
culture.text: Rain fills "the river of God" and waters the furrows, softening the soil for the grain.

culture.title: Valleys covered with corn
culture.text: Pastures full of flocks and valleys covered with grain describe a year of abundance.

Psalms 66.audience: Titled "A Song or Psalm," with no author named. It calls all the earth to praise God for bringing Israel through the sea and through trials.

culture.title: Silver tried in the furnace
culture.text: "Thou hast tried us, as silver is tried"—metal was refined by fire to remove impurities.

culture.title: Paying vows
culture.text: The psalmist brings burnt offerings of rams, bullocks, and goats to pay vows made in trouble.

Psalms 67.audience: Titled "on Neginoth, A Psalm or Song." Its opening echoes the priestly blessing, "God be merciful unto us, and bless us; and cause his face to shine upon us" (compare Numbers 6:24–26).

culture.title: The earth yielding increase
culture.text: A good harvest was taken as a sign of God's blessing.

Psalms 68.audience: A psalm of David celebrating God's march from Sinai to his sanctuary. Paul quotes verse 18 in Ephesians 4:8.

culture.title: Rider on the clouds
culture.text: God is the one "that rideth upon the heavens." Canaanite texts call Baal the rider on the clouds; the psalm gives that title to the LORD.

culture.title: A victory procession
culture.text: Singers go before, musicians behind, and young women playing timbrels in between—a festive procession to the sanctuary.

culture.title: Leading captives
culture.text: Victorious kings led captives in procession and received tribute from the defeated.

Psalms 69.audience: Titled "upon Shoshannim, A Psalm of David." The New Testament quotes it more than almost any other psalm (John 2:17; 15:25; Romans 15:3; Acts 1:20).

culture.title: Gall and vinegar
culture.text: "They gave me also gall for my meat; and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink." Jesus was offered vinegar on the cross (Matthew 27:34, 48).

culture.title: Song of the drunkards
culture.text: "They that sit in the gate speak against me; and I was the song of the drunkards"—mocked in public and in taverns.

Psalms 70.audience: Titled "A Psalm of David, to bring to remembrance." It repeats, with small changes, Psalm 40:13–17.

culture.title: Aha, aha
culture.text: "Aha, aha" was a taunt of gloating enemies (Psalm 35:21).

Psalms 71.audience: Psalm 71 has no title. It is the prayer of an older person: "Cast me not off in the time of old age" (Psalm 71:9).

culture.title: Praise on the psaltery
culture.text: The psaltery (a harp or lyre) accompanied praise of "the Holy One of Israel," a title found often in Isaiah.

Psalms 72.audience: Titled "A Psalm for Solomon," it prays for the king's just rule. It ends Book II with a doxology and the note, "The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended" (Psalm 72:20).

culture.title: Kings of Tarshish and Sheba
culture.text: Distant kingdoms—Tarshish in the west, Sheba and Seba in the south—bring gifts, as the queen of Sheba did to Solomon (1 Kings 10:1–10).

culture.title: Rain on mown grass
culture.text: Rain after the grass was cut helped it grow again—a picture of the king's rule refreshing the land.

culture.title: Gold of Sheba
culture.text: Sheba in southern Arabia was famous for gold, frankincense, and spices.

Psalms 73.audience: A psalm of Asaph that opens Book III. The psalmist nearly loses faith seeing the prosperity of the wicked until he goes into the sanctuary (Psalm 73:17).

culture.title: Pride as a necklace
culture.text: "Pride compasseth them about as a chain"—the wicked wear arrogance like jewelry for display.

culture.title: Slippery places
culture.text: Steep, smooth rock paths in the hills could cause a sudden fall.

Psalms 74.audience: A Maschil of Asaph lamenting the destruction of the sanctuary by enemies (Psalm 74:3–8). Many readers connect it with Babylon's burning of the temple in 586 BC.

culture.title: Axes in the carved work
culture.text: Enemies hack the temple's carved wood paneling with axes and hammers, as a woodcutter fells trees.

culture.title: Leviathan and the sea
culture.text: God breaks the heads of the dragons and of leviathan—images of sea monsters, often linked to the sea and to Egypt's defeat (Isaiah 51:9–10).

Psalms 75.audience: Titled "Altaschith, A Psalm or Song of Asaph." God declares that he judges at the time he chooses.

culture.title: The cup of wrath
culture.text: "In the hand of the LORD there is a cup, and the wine is red." The cup of God's wrath is a common prophetic image (Jeremiah 25:15).

culture.title: Lifting up the horn
culture.text: Raising the horn was a picture of arrogance and strength, like an animal tossing its head.

Psalms 76.audience: Titled "on Neginoth, A Psalm or Song of Asaph." It celebrates God in "Salem" and Zion (Psalm 76:2), perhaps after a deliverance of Jerusalem.

culture.title: Salem
culture.text: Salem is an old name for Jerusalem, first mentioned with Melchizedek king of Salem (Genesis 14:18).

culture.title: Breaking the weapons
culture.text: God breaks "the arrows of the bow, the shield, and the sword."

Psalms 77.audience: Titled "to Jeduthun, A Psalm of Asaph." In distress, the psalmist remembers the exodus, when God led his people "like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron" (Psalm 77:20).

culture.title: Songs in the night
culture.text: The psalmist remembers his song in the night—singing and meditating in sleepless hours.

culture.title: Footsteps in the sea
culture.text: "Thy way is in the sea... thy footsteps are not known"—the path through the Red Sea left no trace once the water returned.

Psalms 78.audience: A Maschil of Asaph retelling Israel's history from the exodus to David, so that children would "set their hope in God" (Psalm 78:7). Matthew applies verse 2 to Jesus' parables (Matthew 13:35).

culture.title: Teaching children
culture.text: History was passed down by fathers telling their children, from generation to generation.

culture.title: Zoan
culture.text: Zoan (Tanis) was a royal city in the eastern Nile Delta, near where Israel lived in Egypt.

culture.title: Shiloh forsaken
culture.text: God "forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh," referring to the ark's capture by the Philistines (1 Samuel 4).

Psalms 79.audience: A psalm of Asaph lamenting that the nations have defiled the temple and "laid Jerusalem on heaps" (Psalm 79:1). Readers knew this from the Babylonian destruction.

culture.title: Unburied dead
culture.text: Bodies left for birds and beasts with "none to bury them" was the worst disgrace in the ancient world.

culture.title: Sevenfold repayment
culture.text: The psalmist asks God to repay the neighbors "sevenfold"—completely.

Psalms 80.audience: Titled "upon Shoshannimeduth, A Psalm of Asaph." It prays for Joseph, Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh—tribes descended from Rachel.

culture.title: A vine out of Egypt
culture.text: Israel is a vine God brought out of Egypt and planted. Vines were trained on walls and terraces and protected by hedges.

culture.title: The boar out of the wood
culture.text: Wild boars lived in the Jordan thickets and could destroy vineyards.

culture.title: Dwelling between the cherubims
culture.text: God is addressed as the one who dwells between the cherubim above the ark (1 Samuel 4:4).

Psalms 81.audience: Titled "upon Gittith, A Psalm of Asaph." It calls for a trumpet on the new moon and full moon "on our solemn feast day" (Psalm 81:3), likely the feast of tabernacles.

culture.title: Trumpet at the new moon
culture.text: The shofar was blown at the new moon and at feasts (Numbers 10:10). The full moon marked the start of Passover and tabernacles.

culture.title: Removed from the burden
culture.text: "His hands were delivered from the pots"—baskets used to carry clay and bricks in Egypt.

Psalms 82.audience: A psalm of Asaph in which God judges "among the gods" (Psalm 82:1). Jesus quoted verse 6, "Ye are gods" (John 10:34).

culture.title: The divine council
culture.text: Ancient Near Eastern texts describe gods meeting in an assembly. Here God judges the "gods," understood by some as heavenly beings and by others as human judges (Exodus 22:28).

culture.title: Defending the fatherless
culture.text: Kings and judges were expected to protect the poor, the fatherless, and the needy.

Psalms 83.audience: A song of Asaph naming a coalition of Israel's enemies: Edom, Ishmaelites, Moab, Hagarenes, Gebal, Ammon, Amalek, Philistines, Tyre, and Assur (Psalm 83:6–8).

culture.title: Remembering past victories
culture.text: The psalmist recalls the defeats of Sisera and Jabin at the Kishon and of the Midianite leaders Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah, and Zalmunna (Judges 4–8).

culture.title: Stubble before the wind
culture.text: Dry stalks and tumbleweed ("a wheel") are blown across open fields by the wind.

Psalms 84.audience: Titled "upon Gittith, A Psalm for the sons of Korah." It is a pilgrim's song of longing for God's house: "How amiable are thy tabernacles" (Psalm 84:1).

culture.title: Birds nesting at the altar
culture.text: Sparrows and swallows build nests in the temple area, near the altars.

culture.title: The valley of Baca
culture.text: Baca means ‘weeping’ or a kind of balsam tree; it was a dry valley on the pilgrim route that God turns into a place of springs.

culture.title: A doorkeeper
culture.text: The psalmist would rather stand at the threshold of God's house than live in the tents of wickedness.

Psalms 85.audience: Titled "for the sons of Korah." It thanks God for restoring the land and asks for renewed mercy.

culture.title: Bringing back the captivity
culture.text: "Thou hast brought back the captivity of Jacob" can mean restoring fortunes or bringing back exiles.

Psalms 86.audience: Titled "A Prayer of David," the only psalm with that title in Book III. It draws heavily on phrases from other psalms and from Exodus 34:6.

culture.title: The son of thine handmaid
culture.text: A slave born in a household belonged to it for life. Calling oneself "the son of thine handmaid" expresses complete devotion.

Psalms 87.audience: A psalm of the sons of Korah celebrating Zion as the birthplace of peoples from Rahab (Egypt), Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Ethiopia (Psalm 87:4).

culture.title: Rahab as Egypt
culture.text: Rahab here is a poetic name for Egypt (Isaiah 30:7), not Rahab of Jericho.

culture.title: A register of peoples
culture.text: "The LORD shall count, when he writeth up the people"—like a census register listing citizens.

Psalms 88.audience: Titled "upon Mahalath Leannoth, Maschil of Heman the Ezrahite." Heman was a wise man (1 Kings 4:31) and a temple musician. It is the only psalm that ends without any turn to praise or hope.

culture.title: The grave and Sheol
culture.text: The psalmist is counted with "them that go down into the pit," in darkness and in the deeps.

culture.title: Abandoned by friends
culture.text: "Thou hast made me an abomination unto them"—serious illness could make a person an outcast (Leviticus 13:46).

Psalms 89.audience: Titled "Maschil of Ethan the Ezrahite." It recalls God's covenant with David and then laments that the crown has been "profaned... to the ground" (Psalm 89:39). It ends Book III.

culture.title: Tabor and Hermon
culture.text: Tabor and Hermon were prominent mountains in the north of the land.

culture.title: A broken covenant sign
culture.text: The king's crown is cast down and his walls and strongholds broken—signs of a fallen dynasty.

Psalms 90.audience: Titled "A Prayer of Moses the man of God," the only psalm attributed to Moses. It opens Book IV.

culture.title: Threescore years and ten
culture.text: A normal lifespan of seventy or eighty years was the expectation in the ancient world.

culture.title: Grass in the morning
culture.text: Grass grows green after rain and withers by evening in the hot sun—an image of how short life is.

culture.title: A watch in the night
culture.text: "A thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday... and as a watch in the night." Peter echoes it (2 Peter 3:8).

Psalms 91.audience: Psalm 91 has no title. The devil quoted verses 11–12 when tempting Jesus (Matthew 4:6).

culture.title: The snare of the fowler
culture.text: Bird catchers used nets and traps. The image is of hidden danger.

culture.title: Pestilence and destruction
culture.text: Plagues and diseases spread quickly in ancient towns. The psalm names "the pestilence that walketh in darkness" and "the destruction that wasteth at noonday."

Psalms 92.audience: Titled "A Psalm or Song for the sabbath day," the only psalm assigned to a specific day in its title.

culture.title: The palm and the cedar
culture.text: The palm tree grows tall in the desert oases and the cedar in the mountains of Lebanon—both pictures of long life and strength.

culture.title: Fresh oil
culture.text: "I shall be anointed with fresh oil"—newly pressed olive oil was used for honor and refreshment.

Psalms 93.audience: Psalm 93 has no title. It begins "The LORD reigneth," the first of several psalms celebrating God as king (Psalms 93; 96–99).

culture.title: The floods lifting up
culture.text: In ancient Near Eastern thought, the raging sea was a symbol of chaos. God is mightier than the waves.

Psalms 94.audience: Psalm 94 has no title. It calls on God as judge against those who oppress the widow, the stranger, and the fatherless (Psalm 94:6).

culture.title: God who made the ear
culture.text: "He that planted the ear, shall he not hear?"—an argument against the idea that God does not see injustice.

Psalms 95.audience: Psalm 95 has no title. It calls worshippers to come before God and warns them not to harden their hearts as at Meribah. Hebrews 3–4 quotes it at length.

culture.title: Meribah and Massah
culture.text: The "provocation" and "temptation" refer to Meribah and Massah, where Israel quarreled over water (Exodus 17:7).

culture.title: Kneeling in worship
culture.text: "Let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker"—postures of reverence before a king.

Psalms 96.audience: Psalm 96 has no title, but most of it appears in the song sung when David brought the ark to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:23–33).

culture.title: Gods that are idols
culture.text: "All the gods of the nations are idols"—the Hebrew word suggests ‘worthless things.’

culture.title: Bringing an offering into his courts
culture.text: Visitors to a king brought gifts. Worshippers brought offerings into God's courts.

Psalms 97.audience: Psalm 97 has no title. It celebrates the LORD's reign with clouds, darkness, fire, and lightning, as at Sinai.

culture.title: Hills melting like wax
culture.text: Wax melts quickly near fire—an image of the earth's mountains before God (Micah 1:4).

Psalms 98.audience: Titled simply "A Psalm." It calls all the earth to sing a new song as God comes to judge the world. Isaac Watts' hymn ‘Joy to the World’ is based on it.

culture.title: Trumpets and cornets
culture.text: Silver trumpets and the shofar (cornet) were blown when a king was acclaimed.

culture.title: Floods clapping their hands
culture.text: Rivers clap and hills sing for joy—creation joining the people's acclamation.

Psalms 99.audience: Psalm 99 has no title. It names Moses, Aaron, and Samuel as those who called on God and were answered (Psalm 99:6).

culture.title: His footstool
culture.text: The ark was called God's footstool (1 Chronicles 28:2). Kings' thrones in the ancient Near East had footstools.

culture.title: The cloudy pillar
culture.text: God spoke to Moses and Aaron "in the cloudy pillar" (Exodus 33:9).

Psalms 100.audience: Titled "A Psalm of praise," in the Hebrew ‘a psalm for thanksgiving,’ perhaps sung when bringing the thank offering. It calls all lands to enter God's gates with thanksgiving.

culture.title: Entering gates and courts
culture.text: Worshippers passed through the temple gates into its courts, where offerings were brought.

culture.title: The sheep of his pasture
culture.text: Kings in the ancient Near East were often called shepherds of their people; here the people belong to God's flock.
